title: Raising and escalating concerns
blurb: Know when and how to raise a concern, the NMC's four stages, and the protection whistleblowers have.
question: A nurse on a night shift is told by the nurse in charge to look after twelve patients on her own as well as cover the high-dependency bay, which she has not been trained for. What should she do?

teach.h: A professional duty, not a choice
teach.body: Every registrant has a professional duty to put the interests of people first and to act if they may be at risk. Code 16 says act without delay if you believe there is a risk to patient safety or public protection, and raise and, if necessary, escalate concerns. Plain English: if something is unsafe, say so, to the right person, and keep going until it is dealt with. The NMC says doing nothing is unacceptable, and failing to report can put your own registration at risk.
teach.cite: NMC Code 16; NMC Raising concerns guidance (2020)

steps.label: 1. Line manager
steps.sub: verbally or in writing; keep a record

steps.label: 3. Higher level
steps.sub: e.g. director of nursing, chief executive

teach.caption: Based on the tiered approach in the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998. You may go to stage 3 from the start if you cannot use stages 1 or 2.

teach.body: If you witness or suspect a risk of immediate harm to a person in your care, report it straight away to the appropriate person or authority and act to protect them. Concerns about abuse or neglect go through local safeguarding procedures first. You do not need all the facts or proof: you need a reasonable belief that wrongdoing is happening, has happened or is likely to happen.

items: 16.1 Raise and escalate concerns about safety or the level of care, using the channels available.
16.2 Raise concerns immediately if asked to practise beyond your role, experience and training.
16.4 Acknowledge and act on concerns raised to you.
16.5 Do not obstruct, intimidate or victimise anyone who wants to raise a concern.
16.6 If you manage others, protect them from harm or detriment after they raise a concern.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Staff Nurse Priya on a medical ward
teach.body: On a night shift Priya is asked to cover the high-dependency bay as well as her twelve patients, with no HDU training. Under Code 16.2 she tells the nurse in charge at once that this is beyond her competence and unsafe, and asks for the bay to be covered by a trained nurse. When nothing changes, she escalates to the site manager, completes an incident report and keeps a written note of who she told and when.

children.label: Freedom to Speak Up Guardian
children.sub: over 1,000 across the NHS and others

teach.caption: The National Guardian's Office closed on 30 June 2026; local Freedom to Speak Up Guardians continue.

head: Law
What it does
rows: Protects workers who raise concerns from detriment or dismissal
Disclosure must be in the public interest
Protects disclosures to regulators such as the NMC
Students on NMC-approved courses protected when disclosing to the NMC
teach.caption: Going to the media or an MP first is protected only in the most extreme circumstances.

teach.text: Don't confuse a CONCERN (you are a witness to risk to others: use the whistleblowing route) with a COMPLAINT or grievance (about how you are treated). And don't go to the media first: use internal routes and regulators before any wider disclosure.

items: Act without delay on risk; immediate risk of harm is reported straight away.
Stages: line manager, designated person, higher level, regulator or helpline.
Give your name if you can: it helps investigation and gives the best legal protection.
Keep a written record; get advice from Protect, a union or a Freedom to Speak Up Guardian.

summary: You can now explain the professional duty to raise concerns, follow the NMC's four-stage route and recognise when immediate action is needed. You also know the difference between a concern and a complaint, and the legal protection for whistleblowers.

A.q: Under NMC guidance, who should a nurse normally raise a concern with first?
options: The Care Quality Commission
The Nursing and Midwifery Council
Her line manager
A local newspaper
A.why: Stage 1 of the NMC guidance is normally to raise the concern internally with your line manager, verbally or in writing.

whyNot.0: The CQC is stage 4, used when internal routes have failed or cannot be used.
whyNot.1: The NMC is a regulator, used later or for concerns about individual registrants.
whyNot.3: The media is a last resort, protected only in the most extreme circumstances.

A.q: What level of certainty does a nurse need before raising a concern?
options: A reasonable belief that wrongdoing may be occurring
Written statements from at least two other witnesses
Confirmation from her manager that the concern is valid
Evidence that a patient has already come to harm
A.why: NMC guidance: you do not need all the facts to prove your concern, but you must have a reasonable belief that wrongdoing is happening, took place or is likely to happen.

whyNot.1: Witness proof is not needed to raise a concern.
whyNot.2: Waiting for a manager to validate it is not required and may delay action.
whyNot.3: Harm does not need to have happened; risk of harm is enough.

A.q: A nurse is asked to give an intravenous medicine she has not been trained to give. What does Code 16.2 require?
options: Give it under supervision this once
Raise her concern immediately
Give it and record that she was asked
Raise it at her next appraisal
A.why: Code 16.2: raise your concerns immediately if you are being asked to practise beyond your role, experience and training. Code 13.3 adds asking for help from someone competent.

whyNot.0: Giving an IV medicine without training is practising beyond competence.
whyNot.2: Recording the request does not make an unsafe act safe.
whyNot.3: Waiting for an appraisal fails the requirement to raise it immediately.

B.q: A nurse wishes to raise a concern but fears being identified. What does the NMC recommend?
options: Report anonymously, since giving a name offers no benefit
Raise it through a relative so that her name is hidden
Wait until she has left the organisation to raise it
Give her name and ask at the outset for confidentiality
B.why: The NMC recommends giving your name: it makes investigation easier and gives the best legal protection. If you want confidentiality, say so at the start, accepting there may be limits.

whyNot.0: Anonymous concerns are much harder to investigate, which affects public safety.
whyNot.1: Using a relative adds no protection and delays action.

B.q: A nurse is unhappy that her annual leave request was refused unfairly. Which route should she use?
options: The raising concerns policy
The grievance procedure
The Freedom to Speak Up Guardian
The CQC staff helpline
B.why: A complaint about how you personally have been treated at work is handled through the employer's grievance or complaints procedure, not the raising concerns route.

whyNot.0: Raising concerns is for risks or wrongdoing affecting others, where you act as a witness.
whyNot.2: Speaking up routes are for concerns about care or wrongdoing rather than a personal leave grievance.
whyNot.3: The CQC helpline is for concerns about providers' care, not personal employment issues.

B.q: A nurse sees a colleague slap a resident with dementia in a care home. What should she do first?
options: Protect the resident and report it straight away
Note it and raise it at the next supervision
Speak privately to the colleague later that shift
Email the CQC from home that evening
B.why: Where there is an immediate risk of harm, act straight away to protect the person and report under local safeguarding procedures (NMC Raising concerns paras 7, 22; Code 17.1).

whyNot.1: Waiting for supervision leaves the resident at risk.
whyNot.2: A private word later does not protect the resident or follow safeguarding procedures.
whyNot.3: Immediate protection and local safeguarding come first; the CQC is a later stage.

C.q: Nurse Tom raised a concern about repeated unsafe staffing with his ward manager and then the designated person. Six weeks later nothing has changed. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Raise it with the director of nursing
Post details on a nursing forum to gain support
Contact a journalist about patient safety
Accept the outcome, as two stages are complete
C.why: Stage 3 is to take the concern to a higher level in the organisation, such as the director of nursing or chief executive, when stages 1 and 2 have not dealt with it.

whyNot.1: Posting online risks confidentiality and is not a recognised route.
whyNot.2: External disclosure to the media is protected only in the most extreme circumstances.
whyNot.3: If the risk persists, the duty is to escalate further.

C.q: A student nurse sees a registered nurse giving medicines without checking identity bands. What should the student do?
options: Wait until she qualifies before reporting what she saw
Ask the patients to check their own identity bands
Discuss it with the patients' relatives at visiting
Inform her practice supervisor or tutor immediately
C.why: NMC guidance applies to students: inform your mentor (now practice supervisor), tutor or lecturer immediately if you believe someone may be put at risk of harm.

whyNot.0: Students have the same duty to act; waiting leaves patients at risk.
whyNot.1: Patients cannot be made responsible for the nurse's safety checks.
whyNot.2: Relatives are not an appropriate route for a professional concern and this risks confidentiality.

C.q: A ward manager learns that a nurse has raised a concern about her leadership. Which response breaches the Code?
options: Acknowledging the concern and explaining next steps
Asking HR for advice on handling the process
Moving the nurse to night shifts as a result
Keeping the nurse updated on progress
C.why: Code 16.5 and 16.6: do not obstruct, intimidate or victimise anyone raising a concern, and protect staff you manage from detriment after a concern is raised. Changing shifts as a result is detriment.

whyNot.0: Acknowledging and acting on concerns meets Code 16.4.
whyNot.1: Seeking HR advice is reasonable and supports a fair process.
whyNot.3: Keeping the person updated is good practice for leaders.

reteach.title: Raising concerns as a ladder
reteach.question: If the first rung does not hold, where do you step next?

blocks.body: Rung 1 is your line manager. If you cannot go to them, or they do not act, step to rung 2 (the designated person in your whistleblowing policy), then rung 3 (a senior leader such as the director of nursing), then rung 4 (a regulator such as the CQC). If someone is in immediate danger, skip the ladder: protect them and report straight away.

blocks.text: Keep a written record at every rung: who you told, when, and an outline of the concern, while protecting patient confidentiality.

explain.body: Code 16: act without delay on risks to safety. Failure to report concerns may bring your own fitness to practise into question.

items.label: beyond your role? raise it now

test.q: According to the NMC, what may happen if a nurse fails to report a concern about patient safety?
options: Her employer becomes liable instead
Her fitness to practise may be questioned
Her revalidation is postponed
Her concern passes to the next shift
test.why: NMC guidance: failure to report concerns may bring your fitness to practise into question and put your registration at risk.

whyNot.0: The nurse's professional duty is personal and does not transfer to the employer.
whyNot.3: The duty to report stays with the nurse who knows of the risk.

explain.body: Line manager, designated person, higher level, then regulator or helpline. Get advice before going outside, and tell your employer what you are doing.

test.q: In England, which body could a nurse contact at stage 4 about a concern with a care provider?
options: The local police station
Her trade union branch
The Care Quality Commission
The hospital chaplaincy team
test.why: Stage 4 is a regulatory organisation or helpline; in England the CQC has a route for staff to raise concerns about providers.

whyNot.0: The police deal with crime, not as the stage 4 regulator for care concerns.
whyNot.1: Unions give advice and support but are not the regulator.
whyNot.3: A chaplain offers pastoral support, not regulation.

explain.body: PIDA 1998 protects workers who make disclosures in the public interest from detriment and dismissal. Disclosures to regulators like the NMC are protected.

test.q: Which Act protects nurses who raise genuine concerns in the public interest from victimisation or dismissal?
options: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974
Care Act 2014
Equality Act 2010
Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998
test.why: PIDA 1998 protects workers who raise genuine concerns about wrongdoing in the public interest and are victimised or dismissed for it.

whyNot.0: HASAWA sets workplace safety duties, not whistleblowing protection.
whyNot.1: The Care Act covers adult care and safeguarding.

explain.body: Protect gives confidential whistleblowing advice; unions and professional bodies can represent you; Freedom to Speak Up Guardians support workers to speak up.

test.q: A nurse wants confidential, independent advice before deciding whether to blow the whistle. Which organisation does the NMC name?
options: Protect
NHS Resolution
Healthwatch
The Patients Association
test.why: The NMC recommends the independent whistleblowing charity Protect, alongside professional bodies and trade unions, for confidential advice.

whyNot.1: NHS Resolution handles claims against the NHS, not staff whistleblowing advice.
whyNot.2: Healthwatch represents patients and the public.
whyNot.3: The Patients Association is a patient charity, not a whistleblowing advice service for staff.
